summary: Specifies the CLUE protocol, an application protocol that lets telepresence endpoints describe and negotiate a session. It builds on the requirements and framework produced by the IETF CLUE working group. It is an experimental specification and has a companion signaling document, RFC 8848.

plainLanguage.summary: Two video rooms need a way to talk about their cameras and screens before the meeting begins. This document defines the conversation they have, so they can agree on who shows what.

questions: how do telepresence endpoints negotiate streams
what is the difference between a media provider and media consumer
what is a media capture in clue
subtitle: Telepresence endpoints describe and negotiate media streams over SCTP-over-DTLS.

tldr.problem: Session Description Protocol (SDP) alone cannot describe the richness of telepresence sessions: what cameras and screens are available, which captures can be simultaneous, how content is grouped, and what a room's spatial layout looks like. Endpoints need a way to negotiate these capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: CLUE defines an application protocol where a Media Provider advertises its available media captures (cameras, screens, layouts) and constraints, and a Media Consumer requests specific captures and encodings. Messages are XML-based and flow over a reliable SCTP-over-DTLS data channel established separately from media.
tldr.outcome: Telepresence endpoints can achieve better 'being there' rendering by coordinating which streams are sent and how they map to physical locations, group constraints, and capture metadata defined in the CLUE data model.

today: RFC 8847 is an Experimental specification defining version 1.0 of the CLUE protocol. It works together with companion RFCs: 8845 (framework), 8846 (data model), 8848 (signaling), and 8850 (data channel). CLUE is not yet widely deployed but is designed for standardization-track advancement pending implementation experience and interoperability testing.

sections.title: The Telepresence Problem
sections.content:
In telepresence sessions, endpoints often have multiple cameras covering different views and screens showing different content. SDP alone cannot express which captures can be sent simultaneously, how captures relate to physical spaces, or group constraints (e.g., 'speaker camera and speaker screen cannot both be sent at full resolution'). CLUE (Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence) is an application protocol that lets a Media Provider advertise its telepresence capabilities and a Media Consumer request desired streams.

CLUE messages are XML-based and flow over an SCTP-over-DTLS data channel, independent of the media streams themselves. The protocol is designed around the CLUE data model and framework defined in companion RFCs 8845 and 8846, and SIP/SDP integration is covered in RFC 8848.
sections.plainLanguage: Video rooms have lots of cameras and screens, and they need a way to tell each other which streams are available and which ones can be sent at the same time.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The CLUE protocol has three main communication phases. First, the CLUE data channel (SCTP-over-DTLS) is established. Second, the endpoints negotiate protocol version and extensions via 'options' and 'optionsResponse' messages. Third, Media Providers advertise their capabilities and Media Consumers request streams.

Each endpoint can act as both a Media Provider (sending captures) and a Media Consumer (receiving captures), leading to two separate message exchange sequences per call. The protocol uses XML messages with mandatory elements (clueId as optional string identifier, sequenceNr as mandatory positive integer) and version/protocol attributes. Each endpoint maintains independent sequence number streams for initiation-phase messages, messages sent as an MP, and messages sent as an MC.
sections.plainLanguage: First the rooms set up a secure connection, then they agree on which protocol version and features to use, then they describe what they can share.

sections.title: CLUE Protocol Messages
sections.content:
The CLUE protocol defines six core messages. 'options' is sent by the Channel Initiator to declare which protocol versions, extensions, and roles (Media Provider, Media Consumer) it supports. 'optionsResponse' is the reply from the Channel Receiver, selecting the common version and extensions and declaring its own roles. 'advertisement' is sent by an MP to advertise media captures, encoding groups, capture scenes, simultaneity constraints, global views, and represented participants. 'ack' is sent by an MC to acknowledge an advertisement. 'configure' is sent by an MC to select desired capture encodings from the advertisement. 'configureResponse' is the MP's reply indicating success (code 200) or failure (codes 3xx or 4xx).

Response codes follow an HTTP-like convention: 2xx for success, 3xx for syntax errors, 4xx for semantic errors. For example, 402 means invalid sequencing, 404 means advertisement expired, 405 means subset choice not allowed for a Multiple Content Capture.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are: 'options' (here is what I can do), 'optionsResponse' (I agree, and here is what I can do), 'advertisement' (these are my cameras and screens), 'ack' (I got that), 'configure' (send me these streams), and 'configureResponse' (okay or no).

sections.title: Protocol State Machines
sections.content:
CLUE participants follow a hierarchical state machine. At the top level, a CP moves from IDLE to CHANNEL SETUP when establishing the SCTP-over-DTLS channel, then to OPTIONS state for version negotiation, and finally to ACTIVE state where MP and MC sub-state machines run independently.

A Media Provider in ADV state prepares an advertisement. After sending it, it moves to WAIT FOR ACK and waits for an acknowledgment. If a 'configure' arrives, it moves to CONF RESPONSE state. If processing succeeds, it sends a 200 'configureResponse' and moves to ESTABLISHED. If telepresence settings change, the MP returns to ADV state to send a new advertisement.

A Media Consumer in WAIT FOR ADV state waits for an advertisement. Upon receiving one, it moves to ADV PROCESSING. It can then send an 'ack' and move to CONF state to prepare the configure, or send 'configure+ack' and move directly to WAIT FOR CONF RESPONSE. After receiving a successful configureResponse, it reaches ESTABLISHED state.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints follow a dance: they set up the connection, agree on what to talk about, then the provider describes what it has, the consumer picks what it wants, and the provider either says yes and sends it or says no and waits for a new request.

sections.title: Versioning and Extensions
sections.content:
The CLUE protocol uses semantic versioning with major and minor components. Major version changes indicate non-interoperable changes. Minor versions are backward compatible: a sender using version 1.5 can always fall back to 1.4 when talking to a 1.4 speaker. All CLUE messages are XML compliant to an XML schema identified by the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:clue-protocol. RFC 8847 defines version 1.0 of this schema.

Extensions allow new protocol features and data model information without changing the core schema. Extensions are negotiated during the options phase and must specify a name, an external XML schema reference, and the protocol version they apply to. Protocol-specific extensions add information to existing messages via placeholder elements in namespaces other than the protocol and data model URNs. Data model extensions add information within CLUE-info URN elements. Both CPs must be aware of and support negotiated extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol version ensures endpoints stay in sync. If one side is newer, they can fall back to an older version they both understand. Extensions let new features be added without breaking old implementations.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content:
In a typical telepresence call, Room A (as CI) sends an 'options' message declaring version 1.0, MP and MC capabilities, and no extensions. Room B (as CR) replies with 'optionsResponse' confirming version 1.0 and its capabilities. Room A's MP then sends an 'advertisement' listing its video captures (main camera, presentation screen) with encoding groups and constraints. Room B's MC acknowledges with 'ack'. Room B's MC then sends 'configure' selecting the main camera at 1920x1080 and presentation screen at 1280x720. Room A's MP responds with 'configureResponse' (200 Success). Meanwhile, Room B's MP sends 'advertisement' to Room A's MC, and the reverse negotiation occurs. Both sides can change their offerings mid-call by sending a new 'advertisement', which completely replaces the previous one.

Each side maintains independent sequence numbers for its role: one sequence for options messages, one for MP messages, one for MC messages. Out-of-order or duplicate messages trigger error responses (402).
sections.plainLanguage: Room A says 'here are my cameras and screens', Room B picks which ones it wants, Room A says 'okay' and starts sending them. Then Room B does the same thing the other way.
